newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin takes over as France's prime minister.
newsitem.headline: Jospin takes over as France's prime minister.

text.p: Socialist Lionel Jospin formally took office as France's prime minister on Tuesday and faced the immediate challenge of how to bring Communists into his government without giving them a veto over policy.

Jospin needs the 38 seats won by the Communists in Sunday's election to assure a majority for his leftist alliance in parliament, but he has insisted he will not hand over policy decisions to anyone outside of his Socialist Party.
Communist party officials were however preparing a wish-list of demands to be met before they could agree to participate.

Among them were demands for an immediate 500 franc ($86) increase in the monthly minimum wage to 6,906 francs, a two percentage point cut in the general value added tax of 20.6 percent and bigger cuts in the VAT rate on basic products.

Even before Tuesday's handover of power, Jospin told Communist leader Robert Hue he wanted "a yes or no answer without conditions" on whether the Communists would join the government, a Jospin aide said.
If they accepted, the Communists could have two cabinet ministers and a secretary of state, the aide said.

After meeting Hue, a smiling and relaxed Jospin was driven into the courtyard of the Matignon prime ministerial offices, where he shook hands with his defeated Gaullist predecessor, Alain Juppe, and was ushered inside for the formal handover of power.

The two men met privately for just 13 minutes before Jospin ushered Juppe back into the courtyard. The outgoing prime minister, wearing a fixed smile, waved cursorily to the crowd, ducked into a waiting car and was driven off at speed.
Jospin, who plans to form a government by the end of the week, is likely to make his debut on the world stage on Thursday at a conference of the Socialist International in Malmo, Sweden, aides said.

They said he planned to attend all forthcoming international summits, accompanying conservative President Jacques Chirac with whom he is obliged to "cohabit" during a period of left-right power-sharing.
The move would be a serious attempt to limit the head of state's traditional pre-eminence in the foreign policy realm.

Major international events this month include a European Union summit in Amsterdam on June 16-17 and a summit of the Group of Seven rich nations in the U.S. city of Denver on June 20-22. NATO leaders are due to meet in Madrid on July 8-9.
French stocks finished higher for a second straight day as investors took heart from some encouraging remarks by some Socialist officials about European monetary union.

Hours before Jospin was appointed, Socialist Elisabeth Guigou, who may take the European affairs portfolio, sought to soothe financial markets worries about prospects for the euro currency following Sunday's leftist parliamentary election win.
Asked whether the new government would seek to ensure the euro is created by the target date of January 1, 1999, Guigou told RTL radio: "Of couse we must respect this deadline."
Without waiting for the formal handover, the leader of the country's second biggest trade union fired a warning shot across the bows of the as-yet-unformed government.

Louis Viannet, head of the Communist CGT, urged the new premier to take quick action to raise the national minimum wage and announce an end to privatisation, even before Jospin convenes a planned conference on a cut in working hours and other issues.

"The government must say quickly what it plans to do about the minimum wage. After that, a whole series of issues will have to be negotiated, and will require very vigorous action by workers," Viannet told France-Inter radio.

Jospin was appointed on Monday by Chirac, who had gambled disastrously by calling a parliamentary election 10 months early, misjudging voter anger over record high unemployment and government austerity policies to qualify for the single European currency.

Jospin has served notice he will not consider implementing further austerity measures before the introduction of the euro. He has argued for a more flexible interpretation of the economic targets for joining it. ($ = 5.825 French Francs)
